theorem.statement:
For the frozen testing and mixture optimizations, the requested common sharp frontier does not exist. Put \(t=\min\{\gamma,\alpha+\beta\}\) and
\[
 u_n=\begin{cases}
 n^{-2t/(4t+d)},&d\le 4t,\\
 n^{-4t/(4t+3d)},&d>4t.
 \end{cases}
\]
For every fixed \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma,d,L)\), there are constants \(0<c<C<\infty\) and \(n_0\), depending only on these five class parameters, such that
\[
 c n^{-2\gamma/(4\gamma+d)}\le \rho_n^*\le C u_n,
 \qquad n\ge n_0. \tag{43}
\]
The upper bound is attained by the total test \(\phi_{n,m_n}^{(4)}\) of \(\texttt{def:single-scale-fourth-order-test}\), with
\[
 m_n=\begin{cases}
 \left\lceil n^{2/(4t+d)}\right\rceil,&d\le4t,\\
 \left\lceil n^{4/(4t+3d)}\right\rceil,&d>4t,
 \end{cases}
\]
and with the stipulated non-rejection for \(n<8\). It has size at most \(a_0\) for every \(n\), type-II error at most \(b_0\) above \(C u_n\) for \(n\ge n_0\), arithmetic cost \(O(n+m_n^d)\), and memory cost \(O(m_n^d)\). At the upper-bound transition \(d=4t\), both formulas give \(u_n=n^{-1/4}\), without a logarithmic factor. If \(\alpha+\beta\ge\gamma\) and \(d\le4\gamma\), then \(t=\gamma\) and (43) closes to \(\rho_n^*\asymp n^{-2\gamma/(4\gamma+d)}\).

In contrast, for \(d=\gamma=1\), \(\alpha=1/10\), \(\beta=9/10\), and any fixed \(L\ge2\),
\[
 \frac{r_{\mathrm{test}}(n)}{\rho_n^*}
 \ge c\Lambda_n^{1/4}n^{3/20}\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad
 \frac{r_{\mathrm{mix}}(n)}{\rho_n^*}
 \ge c n^{3/70}\longrightarrow\infty. \tag{44}
\]
Consequently there is no rate \(r_{\mathrm{sharp}}\) that is simultaneously comparable to \(r_{\mathrm{test}}\), \(r_{\mathrm{mix}}\), and \(\rho_n^*\) for every allowed parameter tuple. Thus the lexicographically minimized frozen envelope and the frozen mixture optimization cannot deliver the proposed sharp-radius conclusion. Outside the displayed matching subregion, (43) is the proved upper--lower bracket; its tightness and any logarithms at a genuinely sharp transition remain unresolved.
theorem.proof_tex:
The comparison experiment in \(\texttt{lem:known-propensity-benchmark}\) has critical radius of order \(n^{-2\gamma/(4\gamma+d)}\). Every observational test is a known-propensity test that ignores the supplied function \(e_P\), so the definitions of the two test classes and their critical radii give
\[
 \rho_{n,e}^*\le \rho_n^*.
\]
The lower half of \(\texttt{lem:known-propensity-benchmark}\) therefore yields
\[
 \rho_n^*\ge c n^{-2\gamma/(4\gamma+d)}. \tag{45}
\]
This is an original fixed-\(n\), all-test converse on the unchanged causal class: the cited benchmark uses the point-mass null with \(e\equiv1/2\), \(m_0\equiv3/8\), and \(\tau\equiv1/8\), so every null-prior component has exactly constant CATE, and its sign-mixture alternatives also belong to that same class.

For the other direction, \(\texttt{prop:single-scale-upper}\) proves size and power of the explicit fourth-order statistic in \(\texttt{def:single-scale-fourth-order-test}\), including profiling over \(c\in I\), empty-bin handling, and zero-curvature handling. The deterministic choices displayed in the theorem are the two choices in that proposition's optimization. Hence its power statement and the definition of \(\rho_n^*\) imply
\[
 \rho_n^*\le C u_n. \tag{46}
\]
The same proposition supplies size at most \(a_0\) for all \(n\), type-II error at most \(b_0\) for \(n\ge n_0\), and the stated arithmetic and memory bounds. Equations (45)--(46) prove (43). If \(d=4t\), direct substitution gives
\[
 \frac{2t}{4t+d}=\frac14
 =\frac{4t}{4t+3d},
\]
so this upper-bound transition has no logarithm. If \(\alpha+\beta\ge\gamma\), then \(t=\gamma\); if also \(d\le4\gamma\), the exponents in (45) and (46) coincide, which proves the asserted matching subregion.

It remains to check whether the two proposed deterministic optimizations can represent the critical radius. Fix \(d=\gamma=1\), \(\alpha=1/10\), and \(\beta=9/10\). The already-proved \(\texttt{thm:test-optimization-not-sharp}\) gives
\[
 r_{\mathrm{test}}(n)\ge4\left(\frac{\Lambda_n}{n}\right)^{1/4}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \rho_n^*\le Cn^{-2/5}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\). Division is legitimate because \(\rho_n^*>0\) by the lower bound (45), and it yields
\[
 \frac{r_{\mathrm{test}}(n)}{\rho_n^*}
 \ge c\Lambda_n^{1/4}n^{2/5-1/4}
 =c\Lambda_n^{1/4}n^{3/20}\longrightarrow\infty, \tag{47}
\]
where \(\Lambda_n=\log\{64(n+1)^3/a_0\}\to\infty\).

For the same fixed parameters, \(\texttt{thm:null-supported-converse-fails}\) gives
\[
 r_{\mathrm{mix}}(n)\ge c n^{-5/14}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \rho_n^*\le C n^{-2/5}.
\]
Again using positivity from (45), division gives
\[
 \frac{r_{\mathrm{mix}}(n)}{\rho_n^*}
 \ge c n^{2/5-5/14}=c n^{3/70}\longrightarrow\infty. \tag{48}
\]
Equations (47)--(48) prove (44). If a common \(r_{\mathrm{sharp}}\) were comparable to all three quantities at every allowed tuple, transitivity of two-sided comparison would bound each ratio in (44), a contradiction. The frozen optimizations therefore cannot support the requested common-rate conclusion. The only all-regime statement established by the available valid test and converse is (43), so no sharper exponent or transition logarithm can be asserted outside its matching subregion.
